plan.english: In spring the snow melts, and the man yokes the cattle to the plough. Leading them, he ploughs the field. He holds the firm plough with his own hands, and sweats. Birds follow the plough. He speaks a hymn of praise. Then his wife sows the seed, and the furrow covers it. It rains. When the sun and the rain arrive, the grain grows up, and his heart becomes joyful.

In that year it did not rain. The well dried up. Grief seized the man's heart. The heat burned the field, and the cattle were thirsty. He lifted his own hands and said: "Father Sky, where is the water? Give us rain!" Then Sky heard him. Thunder arrived, and the rain-cloud rose. It rained. The cattle ran to the well, and drank. He became joyful.

"What is this? What is that?" "Look at this field! This is wheat, that is barley. This is the yoke, that is the wagon. How did the grain grow up? The earth gave it roots, the rain gave it water, the sun warmed it. Now the ears of grain are ripening. A hundred grains are in the ear. Let us cut them off! The year is cheerful."

At dawn the man and his wife went out to the field. He cut off the ears of wheat, she carried the load. Then he cut the barley. The sun burned, and he sweated. The daughter carried water around to them, and they drank. The wagon became full. She became tired. The swift horses pulled the wagon. When night arrived, they carried the grain home on the wagon. They sat down by the hearth, and became warm. He said: "Great is the gift of the earth!"

Winter arrives. The snow lies white, and it becomes cold. The cattle stand in the stall, and the sheep lie in the enclosure. The man sits by the hearth together with his wife. The fire burns, and smoke climbs. They eat wheat, barley, garlic and apples, and drink mead. He puts the yoke together, and prepares the plough. He remembers spring. He says: "Winter will go away, spring will arrive."

There were two brothers. Last year this one ploughed the field and sowed the seed. That one lay by the hearth. Rain fell, and the grain grew up and ripened. This one became rich in grain. In winter he ate grain. That one found nothing. He went to his own brother and said: "Brother, give me grain!" The other said: "I ploughed, you lay." He who ploughs eats grain.

When the sun is red at dawn, when the cattle lie down, when the smoke lies flat, then it rains. When the cranes cry, winter comes. When the sparrows sit in the barley, the grain ripens. When thunder comes in spring, the year is cheerful. Whoever watches the cranes is not afraid of the thunder.

It was getting dark. Thunder came. Then a rain-cloud rose above. The barley trembled. The man was standing in the field. Trembling, he cried: "Rain-cloud, do not break the ears of grain! Go away!" It heard him. It went away, and it did not break the ears of grain. It became bright. They were untouched. He was astonished, and became joyful.

Dawn became bright. The shepherd led the cattle out of the cow-stall. The swift he-goat went ahead. The sheep and the horse followed. They came to the pasture. They ate. He sat down and watched them. Then he drove them to the well, and they drank. They became sated. When night arrived, he drove them on to the enclosure.

In the night sleep seized the shepherd. The dog, who hears well, was awake. He heard a wolf in the darkness, and went to the sheep. They trembled. The wolf saw him and fled. The shepherd saw its tracks. The tracks vanished in the marsh. He said: "Good dog, your name is famous!" He gave him a gift.

It was getting dark. The sheep lay in the enclosure. Then a wolf arrived out of the darkness. Then it crept toward them. They trembled. The ram stood up in front. Its eyes were red. The wolf seized him. Then the dog came. The wolf let him go, and fled. The ram's wool was red with blood. The ram lived.

When night arrives, the cattle come. Standing in the enclosure, the cheerful woman milks them. Her daughter milks the sheep. They give much. She says: "Stand, cattle!" They are standing. The man sits. No one comes. They lie down. They are sated.

At dawn the shepherd led ten sheep out. When he drove them to the enclosure, he saw nine sheep. He trembled, and said: "A ram is missing!" Then he went to the marsh and sought the ram there. He caught sight of him in the marsh. Lifting him on his own arms, he carried him to the enclosure. No sheep is missing.
It was getting dark. Lie down, sheep! Lie down, cattle! The watcher is awake. The fire is red. May Sleep seize you! May the wild beast not arrive! May it not see them! It will become bright.

The king had a thousand cattle and a hundred horses, the shepherd had two cattle. A sharp winter arrived. The king's thousand cattle died in the field. The shepherd led his own two cattle into the house, and they lived. In spring the king came to that house. The shepherd gave him mead. The king drank it and became joyful. He gave him a hundred sheep.

"Where are you driving the sheep, brother?" "I am driving them to the well. The field is dry." "Have you seen the wild beast?" "No one has seen him. The dog heard him in the night." "Where do you dwell?" "I dwell near the marsh." "What are you carrying?" "I am carrying wool." "Live, brother! May the gods guard them!"

Pull, cattle! Pull the plough! Bear the yoke! Make the furrow straight! Do not go astray! The heat burns, and we sweat. The man follows you. I sow the seed. May Mother Earth give grain! May the sun warm the seed! Pull, cattle!

Let us cut the ears of grain! Let us transport the load! With many hands the work is swift. The heat burns, and the wheat is dry. The apples are red. Let us eat up the apples and the garlic! Let us speak a hymn of praise! Drink mead, dear one! Eat grain, sister! Let us be joyful!

Hear the word of your father, son! Do not sow the seed in dry earth. When it has rained, sow! Yoke two cattle to the plough. Do not strike them. Make the furrow straight. The birds eat the seed. He who makes the furrow straight eats the grain.

title: A Father's Words on the Herd

plan.english: Know the sheep, son! Lead the cattle to the well. If a sheep is missing, seek it. Do not leave them in the darkness. The dog is your eye in the darkness. If a wild beast arrives, cry out to the dog. Do not tremble. He who is awake guards his own sheep.

Whoever does not work does not eat. To the man who does not plough, the field gives nothing. If there is smoke, there is fire. The wolf wears the wool of the sheep: he is a wolf indeed. A name is fame. The field is the mother of grain. Grain is gold. He who sows a lie eats a lie. The carpenter builds the plough. Punishment follows the lie. He who works receives the wage. The branch grows from the root. You do not eat gold; you eat grain. The eyes see, the hands work, the feet carry. Cattle and men die. Good fame does not die.

title: The Shepherd's Son and the Beast

plan.english: A master's son drove the sheep to the pasture. He cried: "A wild beast has come!" The men arrived there. They caught sight of nothing. He became joyful. Thrice he deceived them. A wild beast indeed came. He cried, and no one heard him. It seized them. Whoever deceives, no one listens to him.
"Father, who nourishes the field?" "Water nourishes it." "Who nourishes the water?" "Sky nourishes it." "Who nourishes Sky?" "There is no one. He is a father to us."

The master said to the son: "I give you the cattle. I give you the field. Plough it, guard them. Do not deceive your brother. Do not steal. Its boundary is firm. Remember the pledge. May good fame be yours!"

The hearth is the heart of the house. At dawn the mother guards the fire. She gives it honey. She sits by the hearth and speaks: "The fire is a god." The daughter listens. It heats them, and smoke climbs. When the fire dies, the hearth is not a hearth.

The man found honey in something hollow. He carried it to his own wife. She put water to the honey. The honey boiled, and became mead. It became tasty. She sipped it. Then guests arrived. The man gave the gods the poured mead. The cheerful guests drank it, and they became joyful.

Wool grows on the sheep. The wool is white. The wife stretches it. She clothes her son in wool. In winter the son wears it, and becomes warm. The wool gives him heat. Her hands are swift. The gift of the sheep is dear.

The mother stood up. The daughter woke. The mother cooks the wheat, and the wheat boils, and they eat. The father yokes the horses. He says to the son: "Drive them to the pasture!" The son drives them. The daughter carries the load. They do their work.

A guest arrived in the night. The master said: "Guest, go inside! Sit down by the hearth! Eat and drink! A guest is dear in the house. Who are you?" The guest said: "A wild beast seized the sheep, and I fled." The master said: "May the gods give you good things!"

Three dear guests came. The master seated them by the hearth. His wife cooked the wheat and the garlic and carried them around. They ate them up and drank mead thrice. They were satisfied. He said: "May Father Sky guard this house!"
It was getting dark. The man and the woman lay down. Sleep seized them. The fire was red. The dog lay at the hearth, and was awake, and guarded them. A bird cried. It became bright. He stood up.

The adorned woman came to the hearth. She went around it. Her mother cried and said: "Daughter, become dear to the husband!" Her brother gave her a gift of gold. The husband gave her honey. She ate it. Then he said: "Woman, become the mistress of this house! May your sons be many! May the hearth stand firm!"

title: Prayer to Father Sky for Rain

plan.english: Father Sky, giver of good things, hear us! Now this field is dry. Mother Earth is thirsty. You who slew the great serpent, give us water! You who split the great rain-cloud, rain on the field! May thunder come, may the grain swell! May the good grain grow up for us, may the well become full! May the horses and the he-goats drink! May the apples be red!

title: Prayer to Mother Earth over the Seed

plan.english: Earth, cover the seed in your arms! Now we sow the seed for you. Give us grain, give us wheat! May it grow up for us, may it not die! May the roots be firm, may the garlic swell! May the ears of wheat be many! May the garlic grow, may the branch grow from the root!

title: Prayer to the Sun over the Ripening Grain

plan.english: Wheel of the sun, warm the field! Ripen the many ears of wheat! Wheel, may you not burn the barley! Wheel, you are great, look upon it. Give heat to the wheat. Give us imperishable fame.

title: Prayer for the Herd at Night

plan.english: Gods, guard the cattle and the sheep! Guard the he-goats and the horses! May they live and be many. May the bear not seize them in the night. May the watcher be awake, may the ram and the he-goat live. May they indeed see Dawn!

Wild beast, go away from the sheep! Do not seize them, do not seize the ram. Do not come to the enclosure or to the cow-stall. I have seen you; you do not see me. Be bound! Go to the marsh. May he flee away into the darkness!

Earth, we give you wheat and barley. We give honey and the poured mead, we give you red apples. Great is your gift. Receive the gift, we are praisers. Give us seed in spring. May you indeed be great and good!

title: Prayer to Fire at the Hearth

plan.english: Fire, god, eat the gift, eat the branches, be bright! Guard the hearth, guard them! Warm us, may it not die! You are dear to the gods!

Dawn, adorned daughter of Sky, shine! You who drive away the great darkness! Lead the cattle out of the cow-stall to the pasture. May they live and be many. May they see you, behind you the sun follows.
